outputs.L1: We introduce a new class of “random” subsets of the natural numbers, called WM sets. This class includes normal sets, namely sets whose characteristic functions are normal binary sequences. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the solvability of systems of linear equations within every WM set and within every normal set. We further show that any partition-regular system of linear equations with integer coefficients is solvable in every WM set.
outputs.L2: We define a new category of pseudo-random subsets of the natural numbers, called WM sets. This category includes all normal sets, meaning those whose indicator functions form normal binary sequences. We prove exact criteria for when systems of linear equations can be solved inside every WM set and inside every normal set. In addition, we demonstrate that any partition-regular system of linear equations with integer coefficients has a solution in every WM set.
outputs.L3:
The text introduces **WM sets** as a new class of “random” subsets of the natural numbers. These sets are designed to capture a notion of randomness broad enough to include important previously studied examples, while still being structured enough to support strong results in Ramsey theory and additive combinatorics.

A key feature of WM sets is that they include **normal sets**. A normal set is a subset of the natural numbers whose characteristic function is a normal binary sequence; that is, every finite binary block occurs in the sequence with the expected limiting frequency. In this sense, normal sets represent a classical and well-understood model of randomness, and the fact that they fall within the broader class of WM sets shows that WM sets generalize this familiar concept.

The authors study the solvability of systems of linear equations inside these random-like sets. More precisely, they determine **necessary and sufficient conditions** under which a given system of linear equations can be solved within every WM set. This provides a complete characterization of which linear systems are guaranteed to have solutions in all sets belonging to this new class.

In addition, the authors obtain an analogous characterization for **normal sets**. They establish necessary and sufficient conditions for when systems of linear equations are solvable within every normal set. Thus, the paper not only develops the general theory of WM sets but also sharpens our understanding of linear configurations inside classically random subsets of the natural numbers.

One of the main consequences of these results is that **every partition-regular system of linear equations with integer coefficients is solvable in any WM set**. Since partition-regular systems are those that admit monochromatic solutions under every finite coloring of the natural numbers, this result shows that WM sets are rich enough to contain solutions to all such systems. In particular, WM sets behave, with respect to partition-regular linear configurations, like large combinatorial sets despite their random nature.
outputs.L4:
This work introduces **WM sets**, a new class of “random-like” subsets of the natural numbers, and investigates the extent to which such sets contain solutions to systems of linear equations. WM sets are defined through a weak mixing-type property and are shown to include the classical class of **normal sets**, which arise from normal binary sequences and are often regarded as deterministic examples of random behavior. In this sense, WM sets provide a broader framework for studying arithmetic and combinatorial patterns inside subsets of the natural numbers that behave randomly in a measurable or ergodic sense.

The central focus of the text is the solvability of systems of linear equations whose variables are required to lie in a given WM set or normal set. The study asks when a system of integer-coefficient linear equations must have solutions inside such a set, and how this question relates to classical notions from Ramsey theory and partition regularity. A system is called partition regular if, whenever the natural numbers are finitely colored, one color class contains a solution to the system. Partition regular systems are known to capture many fundamental combinatorial configurations, such as arithmetic progressions and other linear patterns.

The text establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for systems of linear equations to be solvable in WM sets and in normal sets. These criteria identify precisely which algebraic constraints allow one to guarantee the existence of solutions inside these random-like sets. In particular, the results show that WM sets are rich enough to contain solutions to every partition-regular system of linear equations with integer coefficients. Since normal sets are contained within the class of WM sets, this also clarifies the arithmetic structure present in normal sets and demonstrates that they possess a strong form of combinatorial largeness.

Overall, the work broadens the understanding of how random-like subsets of the natural numbers support structured arithmetic configurations. By connecting weak mixing behavior, normality, linear equations, and partition regularity, it shows that sets exhibiting randomness can nevertheless contain a wide range of deterministic algebraic patterns. This contributes to the larger study of the interaction between ergodic theory, Ramsey theory, and additive combinatorics.
outputs.L5:
**This** is a simple word, but it carries a lot of meaning. It helps us point to something specific, whether it is an object, an idea, a moment, or a feeling. When we say “this,” we bring attention to what is close, important, or happening right now.

In everyday language, **this** creates clarity. For example, “This book is interesting” tells us exactly which book is being discussed. “This is a good idea” shows approval of a particular thought or suggestion. The word connects the speaker to the present moment and helps the listener understand what matters most.

**This** can also be powerful in writing. It can make a message feel direct and personal. Phrases like “This is your chance” or “This moment matters” encourage people to focus and take action. Although it is a small word, **this** often gives sentences strength, direction, and purpose.

In short, **this** is more than just a common word. It is a useful tool for communication, helping us identify, explain, and emphasize the things that are most relevant.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main contributions of a paper about WM sets, normal sets, and solvability of systems of linear equations in random subsets of the natural numbers.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main contributions can be summarized as follows:

- **It connects three notions of “random-like” subsets of** \(\mathbb N\):  
  1. genuinely random subsets,  
  2. **normal sets**, whose characteristic sequences are normal binary sequences, and  
  3. **WM sets**, sets arising from weakly mixing dynamical systems.

- **It studies when systems of linear equations are solvable inside such sets.**  
  Given a finite system of linear equations, the paper asks whether one can find solutions whose coordinates all lie in a prescribed subset of the natural numbers, especially when that subset behaves randomly.

- **It shows that weak mixing provides enough pseudorandomness to force linear configurations.**  
  WM sets are proved to contain solutions to broad classes of linear systems, often the same kinds of systems one expects to be solvable in genuinely random sets of positive density.

- **It relates normality to additive-combinatorial richness.**  
  Normal sets, although defined by digit-frequency conditions, are shown to contain many linear patterns. The paper clarifies how far normality alone can go in guaranteeing solvability of linear systems.

- **It gives deterministic analogues of probabilistic results.**  
  Instead of relying only on random subsets of \(\mathbb N\), the paper identifies structured deterministic classes — especially WM and normal sets — that still exhibit random-like behavior with respect to linear equations.

- **It connects ergodic theory, number theory, and Ramsey/additive combinatorics.**  
  The arguments use dynamical ideas such as weak mixing and recurrence to prove statements about solutions to linear equations in subsets of the natural numbers.

- **It helps characterize which linear systems are forced by randomness-like assumptions.**  
  The paper contributes to understanding the boundary between systems that necessarily have solutions in random or pseudorandom sets and those that require stronger algebraic or density assumptions.

In short, the paper shows that WM sets and, to a significant extent, normal sets behave like random subsets of the natural numbers with respect to the existence of solutions to finite systems of linear equations. It provides a bridge between probabilistic intuition and deterministic recurrence phenomena.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a math research article introducing WM sets and studying which linear equation systems are solvable in every WM or normal set.
counterfactuals.output: We introduce **WM sets**, a class of subsets of the integers arising from weak-mixing phenomena, and investigate their Ramsey-theoretic behavior with respect to systems of linear equations. The central question is to determine which finite linear systems are guaranteed to have solutions inside every WM set, and, in parallel, inside every normal set. We establish structural criteria characterizing solvability in these classes, relating the answer to classical notions such as partition regularity and density-based largeness. Our results show that WM and normal sets support a rich but sharply constrained family of linear configurations, clarifying the extent to which randomness and weak mixing force arithmetic patterns.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What are the key results of the paper on random subsets of natural numbers, normal binary sequences, and partition-regular linear systems?
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s key results can be summarized as follows:

- **Random subsets and normal binary sequences are linked.**  
  A subset \(A\subseteq \mathbb N\) can be encoded by its characteristic binary sequence. For a genuinely random subset obtained by independently choosing each integer with probability \(1/2\), the resulting binary sequence is almost surely **normal**: every finite binary block occurs with the expected limiting frequency.

- **Normality gives density but not full additive randomness.**  
  If a binary sequence is normal, then the corresponding set of \(1\)’s has asymptotic density \(1/2\), and more generally finite local patterns occur with the expected frequencies. However, normality alone does not guarantee that the set behaves randomly with respect to all additive or linear configurations.

- **Finite partition-regular linear systems persist in random/normal sets.**  
  For many finite homogeneous linear systems that are partition regular over \(\mathbb N\), especially irredundant systems satisfying Rado-type conditions, positive density is enough to force solutions. Since normal sets have density \(1/2\), such systems have solutions inside normal sets, and random subsets almost surely contain such configurations.

- **Infinite partition-regular systems behave differently.**  
  The paper emphasizes a contrast between finite and infinite systems. Some infinite partition-regular systems, such as those related to Hindman’s finite-sums theorem, require very strong combinatorial structure. A random subset of \(\mathbb N\) almost surely does **not** contain the kind of infinite finite-sums structure needed for these systems.

- **Normality is weaker than Ramsey largeness.**  
  Although every random subset is almost surely normal, and normal sets have the expected block frequencies, normality does not imply that the set is “large” in the sense required by all partition-regular systems. Thus, there are normal sets that fail to support certain infinite partition-regular configurations.

- **Main conceptual conclusion.**  
  The paper separates three notions of largeness:
  1. probabilistic largeness, as in random subsets;
  2. statistical largeness, as in normal binary sequences;
  3. Ramsey-theoretic largeness, as required by partition-regular systems.

  These notions overlap for many finite systems but diverge sharply for infinite systems.

In short: random subsets are almost surely normal and contain solutions to many finite partition-regular linear systems, but neither randomness nor normality guarantees the strong additive structure needed for all, especially infinite, partition-regular systems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a brief research-summary paragraph explaining WM sets, their relation to normal sets, and the solvability of integer-coefficient linear equations within them.
counterfactuals.output: WM sets (weakly mixing sets) are subsets of the natural numbers whose indicator sequence is generic for a weakly mixing measure-preserving system; intuitively, they behave “randomly enough” to exhibit strong recurrence and independence properties. Normal sets—sets coming from normal binary sequences, where every finite block occurs with the expected frequency—form a key class of examples: because Bernoulli shifts are weakly mixing, every normal set is a WM set, though WM sets may be more general than normal sets. A central consequence is that WM sets are rich in additive and linear configurations: for many integer-coefficient linear equations, especially homogeneous equations with nontrivial positive-integer solutions, one can find solutions with all variables lying inside the WM set. Thus WM sets extend the familiar combinatorial largeness of normal sets, showing that weak mixing alone is enough to guarantee solvability of broad families of linear equations within the set.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a short academic abstract for a combinatorial number theory paper proving necessary and sufficient conditions for linear systems to have solutions in all WM sets and all normal sets.
counterfactuals.output: We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a finite system of linear equations with integer coefficients to be solvable inside every WM set and inside every normal set of integers. The criteria are given in terms of the algebraic structure of the coefficient matrix and refine classical partition-regularity phenomena by distinguishing recurrence properties arising from weak mixing and normality. Our proof combines tools from additive combinatorics, ergodic Ramsey theory, and symbolic dynamics, translating largeness properties of sets into multiple-recurrence statements for associated dynamical systems. As consequences, we characterize precisely which linear configurations are unavoidable in these two natural classes of pseudorandom sets and obtain a unified framework encompassing several known results on partition regularity, density, and recurrence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
